item.research_question: What are the tensile and creep properties of Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 high entropy alloy, and how do gravity casting versus suction-assisted casting followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) affect its microstructure and mechanical behavior?
item.processing_route: Vacuum arc melting (4 re-melts), casting into bars (gravity or suction-assisted), followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1230 °C and 152 MPa for 4 h
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile tests, compression tests at room temperature, and creep tests at 982 °C under 200 MPa and 120 MPa loads
key_findings: The HIP process induced the formation of a secondary Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase in addition to the initial Body Centered Cubic (BCC) phase.
Microhardness increased from 323.5 ± 6.5 HV (gravity) and 330.2 ± 9.8 HV (suction) before HIP to 437.2 ± 11.6 HV and 509.1 ± 13.5 HV after HIP, respectively.
The HCP phase was evenly dispersed in the matrix for gravity-cast specimens but concentrated mostly at grain boundaries for suction-assisted cast specimens.
Tensile elongation to fracture was below the machine's detection limit, indicating extreme brittleness at room temperature.
Compression yield strength values were nearly double the maximum stress measured under tension.
Creep tests at 982 °C resulted in premature failure after 15 minutes (at 200 MPa) and 90 minutes (at 120 MPa).
Fractography revealed inter-crystalline brittle fracture with no evidence of plastic deformation in either casting method.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the slow cooling rate during the HIP process allows the high-temperature BCC phase to undergo a eutectoid reaction or precipitation of the HCP component (ZrHf-rich phase), whereas rapid cooling in as-cast conditions results in a supercooled BCC phase. The difference in mechanical properties and hardness is attributed to the distribution of the ZrHf-rich phase and its influence on dislocation mobility, similar to precipitation hardening.
item.limitations: The authors state that the exact mechanism of HCP phase formation requires further research to confirm, and the influence of preexisting surface cracks on the poor creep properties needs further investigation.
item.future_work: Further research is required to confirm the proposed mechanism of HCP phase formation and to investigate the existence, propagation process, and influence of open surface cracks on the poor creep properties of the material under tension.
quotes: The HIP process is responsible for the appearance of a Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase that is dispersed differently in these two castings.
The elongation to fracture under tension was below the machine's detection limit and therefore could not be measured.
High concentration of oxides observed beneath the surface of the broken creep specimens may point to preexisting surface cracks through which the oxidation process occurred.
